summary: Sort an array containing only 0, 1 and 2 in place (the Dutch national flag problem).
mainInsight: With only three distinct values you do not need a comparison sort: either count each value and rewrite (two passes) or maintain three regions with low/mid/high pointers and place each element once (one pass).

approaches.name: Dutch national flag (one pass)
approaches.summary: low/mid/high pointers; swap 0s to the front, 2s to the back, leave 1s.

personalSolution.notes: Correct and O(n). The follow-up asks for a single pass: the Dutch national flag partition.

promptVariants: Which technique sorts a 3-valued array in one pass?
What is the name of the three-pointer partition used for Sort Colors?
cards.explanation: Three regions (0s, 1s, 2s) are grown in place by low/mid/high. (Dutch national flag: three-way partition)

incorrectOptionExplanations.Merge sort: O(n log n) and extra space.

promptVariants: State the invariant of the one-pass three-pointer solution.
What do the regions [0, low), [low, mid), (high, n-1] hold?
cards.answer: [0, low) are all 0s, [low, mid) are all 1s, (high, n-1] are all 2s, and [mid, high] is unprocessed. Each step shrinks the unprocessed region.
cards.explanation: After swapping with high, do not advance mid (the swapped-in value is unseen).

promptVariants: Time complexity of counting sort here: ___
Sort Colors via counting or three pointers is ___ time.
cards.explanation: Two linear passes (counting) or one pass (partition).

promptVariants: Extra space of your counting solution: ___
Counting sort for three colours needs ___ extra space.
How can the two-pass counting solution be turned into a one-pass in-place solution?
Explain the one-pass Dutch national flag update rules for 0, 1 and 2.
cards.answer: Use low/mid/high pointers: on 0 swap with low and advance low and mid; on 1 advance mid; on 2 swap with high and decrement high (without advancing mid). This is the Dutch national flag partition.
keyPoints: Swap 0 to the front, 2 to the back
Do not advance mid after swapping with high
cards.explanation: The follow-up in the problem statement.

promptVariants: Why does counting sort work here even though the problem says 'sort in place'?
Why is the two-pass counting solution legitimate for Sort Colors, and when would it not be?
cards.answer: Only three distinct values exist, so the counts completely describe the sorted result; overwriting nums with the right number of 0s, 1s and 2s reproduces it. The counter array has constant size, so extra space is O(1).
cards.explanation: It is not a general-purpose sort; it relies on the tiny key range.
